catalog_quote: An examination of word-stress placement in the phonemicized vocabulary presented in Siebert (1945) and the phonetic/phonemic data in his notes reveals that stress placement is based on long and short syllables. A syllable is long if it ends with a long vowel, a nasal vowel, or a vowel followed by a consonant; a syllable is short if it ends in a short vowel. Stress falls on the penultimate syllable if it is long. If the penultimate syllable is short, the stress falls on the antepenultimate syllable of trisyllabic or longer words. In disyllabic words, the stress falls on the penultimate if the word is composed of two morphemes. If the word consists of a single morpheme, the stress may fall either on the ultimate or penultimate syllable (9-12). ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Quantity-sensitive right-edge stress (Latin-type): a syllable counts as long/heavy if it has a long vowel, a nasal vowel, or a coda consonant. Stress the penult if it is heavy; if the penult is light, stress the antepenult (words of three or more syllables). In two-syllable words stress is penultimate (initial) when the word is bimorphemic, but varies between final and penultimate when monomorphemic (e.g. wide· 'buffalo', taru· 'big'). Rudes derives this from Siebert's 1941 phonemicized vocabulary and field notes, and notes the system is nearly identical to that reconstructed for Proto-Northern Iroquoian (areal), differing in being syllable-length rather than vowel-length based (n. 24).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress in the recovered Rudes text. Gatschet 1900: 529-530 speaks impressionistically of a 'secondary accent' in words of three or more syllables that 'frequently overwhelms the primary accent of the radix'. HNAI 14 (2004) Catawba orthography marks only a single stress (v́).
new_statements.exceptions: Monomorphemic disyllables: stress on either ultimate or penultimate (example set 12). Rudes also documents inconsistent stress marking in Speck 1934 (same word marked penultimate then antepenultimate in successive sentences); Voorhis 1984: 3-4 judged Speck's accents non-distinctive and 'bound up with intonation' (final accent on sentence-initial/topic nouns, interrogative suffixes usually accented under rising intonation); Gatschet 1900 says accent shifts under 'rhetorical' influence and the deictic suffix -re draws emphasis to the word end.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on citation/phonemicized forms from Siebert's 1941 fieldwork with the last fluent speakers (Sallie Gordon b.1865, Robert L. Harris, Sam Blue; Esaw = Catawba proper and Saraw dialects). Rule refers to morphological composition for disyllables. Text-level accent marks in Speck 1934 reflect phrase intonation per Voorhis. Stress treated as marked in orthography (v́) by HNAI 14 following Siebert 1945 / Rudes 2003.
new_statements.identity_note: Rudes 2003 describes Catawba as recorded by Siebert in 1941 from the last fluent speakers on the Catawba Reservation near Rock Hill SC (Esaw = Catawba proper, and Saraw dialects; Rudes labels some forms '(Esaw)'); this is the language-level entity cata1286 (ISO chc); no separate dialect glottocodes involved. Woccon (the other Catawban language) is not covered.

sources.note: pp. 3-4 (on Speck's 1934 transcriptions): 'In many words in Speck's texts there is apparent random variation in the place of accent: yúksu (1A.6), yuksú (1A.8) 'his mother'. No attempt is made here to discover a basic or phonemic accent.. Indeed, there is no clear evidence that the accents recorded by Speck can ever distinguish otherwise identical words. On the contrary, the many words with varying accent suggest that it is bound up with intonation. A final-syllable accent is especially common on nouns near the beginning of sentences; perhaps it marks a topic.. Final-syllable accents possibly…

sources.citation: Gatschet, Albert S. 1900. Grammatic sketch of the Catawba language. American Anthropologist n.s. 2(3): 527-549.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: 'Accentuation', pp. 529-530: 'the radical syllable be emphasized above all other syllables of a word.. But when a word grows to the length of three syllables or more, a secondary accent manifests itself which frequently overwhelms the primary accent of the radix.. the accent is not so much tied to a single syllable as in European languages; various influences cause it to shift, and then it assumes a rhetorical function. The deictic suffix -re.. is always likely to draw the emphasis to the end of the word'. Impressionistic 1881 fieldwork; Sapir (IJAL 1:85) called the sketch 'worthless'.
